title_vi: Các luồng OAuth 2.0: chọn luồng nào cho ứng dụng nào?

source_snapshot.note: Pinned commit/path body independently hashed as Git blob; computed OID matches provider tree OID. Non-empty source was read; no source-image bytes used.

related.reason_vi: OAuth là ủy quyền chứ không phải đăng nhập; bài đó giải thích luồng mã ủy quyền và PKCE.
Token OAuth đặt cạnh khóa SSH, chứng chỉ và mật khẩu.

claims.evidence: Source read. OAuth 2.1 working-group draft (oauth-wg/oauth-v2-1 at d04b368), OWASP OAuth 2.0 Cheat Sheet (OWASP/CheatSheetSeries at 1c3144a) and authlib 1.9.1 documentation and grant classes (authlib/authlib at 8a308fc) read from pinned GitHub copies. The four flows were run with authlib 1.9.1 on localhost in a throw-away venv with fake credentials, twice with identical output apart from random values. RFC 6749, RFC 7636 and RFC 9700 were not reachable and were not read; statements about them repeat what OWASP and the draft say. Real identity providers were not tried.

claims.claim_vi: The source lists four flows with one short paragraph each: Authorization Code (client receives an authorization code and exchanges it for an access token and refresh token), Client Credentials, Implicit, Resource Owner Password Grant. Its Client Credentials paragraph is word for word the Implicit paragraph (designed for single-page applications; access token returned directly without an intermediate authorization code), and it names the implicit flow 'Implicit Code Flow'.
claims.verified_by: Source body read; the two paragraphs compared sentence by sentence.

claims.claim_vi: The OAuth 2.1 draft says the framework lets an application obtain limited access either on behalf of a resource owner or on its own behalf.
claims.verified_by: Read from a copy fetched from raw GitHub at the pinned commit (sha256 7b36ad71629bb5603ff636768142618244e2b87a4296ef7e3fa555d5715d0bb4). It is a working-group draft, not a published RFC.

claims.claim_vi: The draft defines two client types, confidential (clients with credentials at the authorization server) and public (clients without); it assumes credentials included in a native application can be extracted and that in a browser-based application protocol data and credentials are easily accessible.
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the draft.

claims.claim_vi: In the draft's authorization code flow the client sends the user's browser to the authorization server with its client identifier, code challenge and redirect URI; the authorization server authenticates the resource owner and redirects back with an authorization code; the client requests the token with the code and the code verifier, and receives an access token and optionally a refresh token. The S256 challenge is BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))).
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the draft.

claims.claim_vi: The draft says an authorization server must reject authorization requests without a code_challenge from public clients.
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the draft.

claims.claim_vi: The draft's client credentials grant: the client requests an access token using only its client credentials (or other authentication) for resources under its control or previously arranged with the authorization server; the grant must only be used by confidential clients; the exchange is one authenticated request to the token endpoint and one access token back, with no resource owner step.
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the draft.

claims.claim_vi: The draft defines three grant types (authorization code, refresh token, client credentials) and omits the Implicit grant and the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, citing the security best current practice (RFC 9700) for both.
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the draft. RFC 9700 itself was not reachable and was not read.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP marks the Implicit grant 'deprecated, do not use' (tokens in the URL fragment can be retained in browser history and read by scripts on the response page, and cannot be sender-constrained) and says clients must use the authorization code grant with PKCE for all client types.
claims.verified_by: Read from a copy fetched from raw GitHub at the pinned commit (sha256 cd31d4f3adb876949f1b3090862e88437becd740f3e8d54fd9809b892e82a45d). The RFC 9700 section it cites was not read.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP says the Resource Owner password credentials grant is not used because it insecurely exposes the resource owner's credentials to the client.
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the cheat sheet.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP says PKCE ensures an attacker cannot redeem a stolen authorization code without the code_verifier, enforced by the authorization server, and notes that PKCE protects authorization codes while access and refresh tokens need sender-constrained tokens (DPoP or mTLS).
claims.verified_by: Read from the same copy of the cheat sheet. DPoP and mTLS were not tried.

claims.claim_vi: Authlib's concepts page names four roles (client, resource owner, resource server, authorization server) and the framework's two ways of obtaining access (on behalf of a resource owner, or on the application's own behalf); its documentation says there are four grant types defined by RFC 6749 and that the password grant should be used only when the client is trustworthy.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of the repository at the pinned commit; the password-grant sentence is in docs/oauth2/authorization-server/flask/grants.rst (same commit). RFC 6749 itself was not read.

claims.claim_vi: Authlib's implicit grant class describes the flow as returning the access token as the result of the authorization request (no separate token request), not supporting refresh tokens, and not including client authentication; its client credentials class passes include_refresh_token=False and says the grant must only be used by confidential clients; its authorization code class issues a refresh token only when the client is allowed the refresh_token grant.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of the repository at the pinned commit (implicit.py, client_credentials.py and authorization_code.py).

claims.claim_vi: Observed, authorization code with PKCE for a public client against an authorization server that requires PKCE: the client makes a 43-character code_verifier and a 43-character S256 code_challenge (recomputed independently with hashlib); the authorization request carries 7 parameters (client_id, code_challenge, code_challenge_method, redirect_uri, response_type, scope, state); the user's password is posted to the authorization server, which answers 302 with only code and state; the token request carries client_id, code, code_verifier, grant_type, redirect_uri and returns access_token, expires_in, scope, token_type; the server request log is POST /authorize, POST /token, GET /api/whoami; the client's 6-line transcript does not contain the password and the access token never appears in a redirect URL.
claims.section: Đọc hình: Mã ủy quyền + PKCE
claims.verified_by: Observed by running flows_demo.py (kept in the authoring scratchpad, not in the repository) with authlib 1.9.1, Flask 3.1.3, Werkzeug 3.1.9, requests 2.34.2 on Python 3.13.16 against localhost servers on random ports; the output was identical (apart from random values) in the last two runs. One measurement on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed against the PKCE-requiring server: a stolen code without a verifier gets invalid_request (Missing 'code_verifier'); with a guessed verifier, or with the challenge sent as the verifier, invalid_grant (Code challenge failed); the real client could still redeem the same code afterwards; reusing a redeemed code gets invalid_grant.

claims.claim_vi: Observed against a second server without PKCE support: a stolen code with only client_id and redirect_uri was exchanged for an access token, and the resource endpoint reported user alice for it.

claims.claim_vi: Observed with a confidential web client: the code and verifier without the client secret got 401 invalid_client; code, verifier and the secret in an HTTP Basic header got 200 with access_token, expires_in, refresh_token, scope, token_type. A public client that was not allowed the refresh_token grant got no refresh token.

claims.claim_vi: Observed, client credentials: one authenticated POST /token (fields grant_type and scope, Basic header) and no /authorize request; response keys access_token, expires_in, scope, token_type (no refresh_token although refresh tokens were switched on for the server and issued to other clients); the resource endpoint reported user null and client batch-job; a wrong secret, no client authentication and a public client each got 401 invalid_client.

claims.claim_vi: Observed, implicit: the redirect after the user's login carried the access token in the URL fragment (keys access_token, expires_in, scope, state, token_type; no query, no refresh_token), no /token request was made, and the token worked at the resource endpoint.

claims.claim_vi: Observed, password grant: the client posted username and password to /token (Basic header for the client), the password was present in the client's own transcript, no /authorize request was made, and the response included a refresh_token; a wrong password got 400 invalid_request.

claims.verified_by: Observed by running flows_demo.py (kept in the authoring scratchpad, not in the repository) with authlib 1.9.1, Flask 3.1.3, Werkzeug 3.1.9, requests 2.34.2 on Python 3.13.16 against localhost servers on random ports; the output was identical (apart from random values) in the last two runs. claims.claim_vi: Observed: with the PKCE-requiring configuration, authlib 1.9.1 issued a code for a public client's authorization request that had no code_challenge and rejected the token request only afterwards (Missing 'code_verifier'); the draft says the authorization endpoint must reject such a request. Authlib 1.9.1's authorization code grant also accepted only secret-based client authentication until the 'none' method was added in the experiment, although its documentation lists 'none' as a default.
claims.verified_by: Observed by running flows_demo.py (kept in the authoring scratchpad, not in the repository) with authlib 1.9.1, Flask 3.1.3, Werkzeug 3.1.9, requests 2.34.2 on Python 3.13.16 against localhost servers on random ports; the output was identical (apart from random values) in the last two runs. One measurement on the authoring machine. The default list was read in authorization_code.py and grants.rst at the same commit.

claims.claim_vi: An access token that can be exchanged without the client secret is useless to someone who lacks the secret, but anyone who holds the secret of a client-credentials client can obtain tokens.
claims.verified_by: Author's inference; the experiment showed only that requests without the secret were refused. Not checked against any specification text.

claims.claim_vi: Not examined: the text of RFC 6749, RFC 7636 and RFC 9700, real identity providers, consent screens, OpenID Connect, device authorization, refresh token rotation, DPoP and mTLS-bound tokens, and Backend for Frontend patterns.
claims.verified_by: Not examined.

design_notes_vi: Khung một: bốn thẻ, mỗi thẻ một luồng theo câu hỏi ai có mặt. Khung hai: chuỗi sáu thông điệp cho thấy mã bị trộm vô dụng khi thiếu verifier. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source's Client Credentials paragraph is a copy of its Implicit paragraph (designed for single-page applications, token returned directly); the lesson says client credentials is a client acting for itself with no user, usable only by confidential clients, and shows it with no authorization request and a token whose user is null.
The source calls the implicit flow 'Implicit Code Flow'; the lesson notes the flow has no authorization code (the token comes in the redirect).
The source lists the four flows as equal options; the lesson reports that OWASP calls Implicit deprecated and says not to use the password grant, and that the OAuth 2.1 draft omits both.

The source says the authorization code flow returns an access token and a refresh token; the lesson says the refresh token is optional and shows a public client that was not allowed it receiving none.
The source does not mention PKCE; the lesson adds it as the protection that makes a stolen authorization code useless, as OWASP says clients must use PKCE with the code flow for all client types.
The lesson adds the question of who is present and whether the client can keep a secret as the way to choose a flow, which the source does not discuss.
editorial_note_vi: Bài mới viết trong kho này, chờ review kỹ thuật. Chưa user testing hoặc phê duyệt phát hành.
